questions.text: In “O Me! O Life!”, why does the speaker include himself among the foolish and faithless?
questions.answer: He reproaches his own failings as well as those he sees around him. This self-criticism prevents his complaint from being merely an attack on other people.

questions.text: What contrast is created by the long complaint and the short answer in Whitman’s poem?
questions.answer: The long complaint accumulates disappointment, while the brief answer offers a simple affirmation: life and personal identity exist, and each person can contribute.

questions.text: How does the image of a “powerful play” change the mood of “O Me! O Life!”?

questions.answer: She bears her mother’s physical features and facial expressions, and remembers the example her mother set. The inheritance is both bodily and emotional.

questions.answer: It suggests that her mental clarity has become obscured. The poem does not name a specific medical diagnosis, so one should not be invented.

questions.text: Why is the doctors’ explanation of a fatal joy ironic rather than an unquestionable account of Louise’s thoughts?
questions.answer: The doctors see her collapse but do not know her private sense of liberation. Readers may interpret her death as connected to losing that imagined freedom; the story does not provide a medical diagnosis proving the interpretation.
